notes.definition: Ionic bonding happens when a metal atom transfers electrons from its outer shell to a non-metal atom, forming oppositely charged ions that attract each other strongly.
explanation: When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom, electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positively charged ion, because it now has more protons than electrons. The non-metal atom gains electrons and becomes a negatively charged ion, because it now has more electrons than protons. The number of protons in the nucleus never changes when an ion forms.

The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas (Group 0), with a full outer shell. For example, sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na⁺ (2,8), which has the same electronic structure as neon. Chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to become Cl⁻ (2,8,8), which has the same electronic structure as argon.

You can work out the charge on an ion from the group number. Group 1 metals lose 1 electron and form 1+ ions (Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺). Group 2 metals lose 2 electrons and form 2+ ions (Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺). Group 6 non-metals gain 2 electrons and form 2− ions (O²⁻, S²⁻). Group 7 non-metals gain 1 electron and form 1− ions (F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻). The negative ions are named with the ending -ide: oxide, sulfide, fluoride, chloride, bromide, iodide.

Electron transfer during the formation of an ionic compound can be represented by a dot and cross diagram. Electrons from one atom are drawn as dots and electrons from the other atom as crosses, so you can see where each electron came from. Usually only the outer shells are drawn. The ions are drawn inside square brackets with the charge written at the top right. In the products, the metal ion is shown with a full outer shell (the shell below the one it lost) or with no outer electrons; both are accepted.

The total number of electrons lost by the metal atoms must equal the total number gained by the non-metal atoms. In sodium chloride, one sodium atom gives one electron to one chlorine atom (ratio 1 : 1). In magnesium oxide, one magnesium atom gives two electrons to one oxygen atom (1 : 1). In calcium chloride, one calcium atom gives one electron to each of two chlorine atoms, so the formula is CaCl₂. In sodium oxide, two sodium atoms each give one electron to one oxygen atom, so the formula is Na₂O. The overall charge on an ionic compound is zero.
keyFacts: Ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal.
Electrons are transferred from the outer shell of the metal atom to the non-metal atom.
Metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.
Ions of Group 1, 2, 6 and 7 elements have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
Group 1 → 1+ ion; Group 2 → 2+ ion; Group 6 → 2− ion; Group 7 → 1− ion.
The number of protons does not change when an ion forms; only the number of electrons changes.
Dot and cross diagrams show electrons from different atoms as dots and crosses; ions go in square brackets with the charge outside.
Electrons lost by the metal = electrons gained by the non-metal, so ionic compounds have no overall charge.

keyTerms.definition: An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge because it has lost or gained electrons.
An ion with more protons than electrons, formed when a metal atom loses electrons.
An ion with more electrons than protons, formed when a non-metal atom gains electrons.
The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A diagram showing the outer shell electrons of atoms or ions, with electrons from different atoms drawn as dots and crosses.
A full outer shell of electrons, the same arrangement as an atom of a Group 0 element such as neon or argon.
The movement of electrons from one atom (the metal) to another (the non-metal) when an ionic bond forms.

workedExamples.title: Describing the formation of sodium chloride
workedExamples.question: Describe what happens when sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride. Give the electronic structures of the atoms and ions.
steps: Sodium atom: 2,8,1. It has one electron in its outer shell.
Chlorine atom: 2,8,7. It needs one more electron to fill its outer shell.
One electron is transferred from the outer shell of the sodium atom to the chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes Na⁺ (2,8) and chlorine becomes Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Both have a noble gas electronic structure.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly: this is the ionic bond.
workedExamples.answer: One electron moves from Na to Cl, giving Na⁺ (2,8) and Cl⁻ (2,8,8), which attract each other.

workedExamples.title: Using group numbers to find charges and a formula
workedExamples.question: Potassium is in Group 1 and sulfur is in Group 6. Give the charges on their ions and deduce the formula of potassium sulfide.
steps: One sulfur atom needs 2 electrons, but each potassium atom can only give 1, so 2 potassium atoms are needed.

workedExamples.title: Counting electrons in ions
workedExamples.question: Calcium has atomic number 20. How many protons and electrons does a Ca²⁺ ion have?
steps: Atomic number 20, so a calcium atom has 20 protons and 20 electrons.
The 2+ charge means 2 electrons have been lost.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a positive ion has gained protons.
misconceptions.right: The number of protons never changes. A positive ion has lost electrons, so it has more protons than electrons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think non-metal atoms give electrons to metal atoms.
misconceptions.right: Electrons always go from the metal atom to the non-metal atom.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the ionic bond is the electron transfer itself.
misconceptions.right: The transfer forms the ions; the ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a Group 6 element forms a 6+ or 6− ion.
misconceptions.right: Group 6 atoms have 6 outer electrons and gain 2 to fill the shell, forming 2− ions such as O²⁻.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think magnesium chloride is MgCl because there is one of each element.
misconceptions.right: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions to balance the charge, so the formula is MgCl₂.

realWorld: Sodium chloride (table salt) and potassium chloride (used in low-sodium salt) are ionic compounds formed by electron transfer.
Calcium fluoride (fluorite) forms from calcium and fluorine; fluoride ions in toothpaste come from ionic compounds such as sodium fluoride.
Magnesium oxide forms the bright white ash when magnesium ribbon burns; it is used as a heat-resistant lining in furnaces.
examTips: In dot and cross diagrams, draw ions in square brackets with the charge at the top right, and use dots for one atom's electrons and crosses for the other's.
Make sure every ion in your final diagram has a full outer shell (8 electrons), and that the number of crosses that moved equals the number of electrons lost by the metal.
Use the group number for charge: Groups 1 and 2 give 1+ and 2+; Groups 6 and 7 give 2− and 1−.
When asked to 'describe' the formation, include: electrons transferred, from metal to non-metal, how many, the ions formed with charges, and noble gas structure.
Never say 'protons are lost' or 'the ion gains a charge by gaining protons'.
summary: Ionic bonding: metal atoms transfer outer shell electrons to non-metal atoms.
Metals form positive ions; non-metals form negative ions.
Ions of Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 have a noble gas electronic structure.
Charges: Group 1 is 1+, Group 2 is 2+, Group 6 is 2−, Group 7 is 1−.
Dot and cross diagrams show the transfer, with ions in square brackets.
Electrons lost must equal electrons gained, so the compound is neutral.

flashcards.front: What is transferred in ionic bonding, and in which direction?
flashcards.back: Outer shell electrons, from the metal atom to the non-metal atom.

flashcards.front: Why does a metal atom become a positive ion?
flashcards.back: It loses electrons, so it has more protons than electrons.

flashcards.front: Charge on the ion of a Group 1 metal?
Charge on the ion of a Group 2 metal?
Charge on the ion of a Group 6 non-metal?
Charge on the ion of a Group 7 non-metal?
Electronic structure of Na and Na⁺?
Electronic structure of Cl and Cl⁻?
What is special about the electronic structure of ions from Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7?
flashcards.back: They have the electronic structure of a noble gas (a full outer shell).

flashcards.front: In a dot and cross diagram, how do you show an ion?
flashcards.back: Inside square brackets with the charge at the top right.

flashcards.front: Formula of magnesium chloride and why?
flashcards.back: MgCl₂: one Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ to balance the charge.

flashcards.front: Formula of sodium oxide and why?
flashcards.back: Na₂O: two Na⁺ balance one O²⁻.

flashcards.front: Does the number of protons change when an ion forms?
flashcards.back: No. Only the number of electrons changes.

questions.question: What happens to a sodium atom when it forms a sodium ion?
markScheme: 1 mark: It loses one electron.
questions.explanation: Sodium is a Group 1 metal and loses its single outer electron to form Na⁺. Protons are not lost; sharing is covalent bonding.

questions.question: What is the charge on a bromide ion? Bromine is in Group 7.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1−
questions.explanation: Group 7 atoms have 7 outer electrons and gain 1 more to fill the shell, giving a 1− charge (Br⁻).

questions.question: Which particles are transferred when an ionic bond forms?
markScheme: 1 mark: Electrons
questions.explanation: Only electrons move between atoms in chemical reactions. Protons and neutrons stay in the nucleus.

questions.question: Which ion has the same electronic structure as the noble gas neon (2,8)?
markScheme: 1 mark: Mg²⁺
questions.explanation: Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 electrons to become 2,8. K⁺, Cl⁻ and S²⁻ all have the argon structure 2,8,8.

questions.question: Calcium is in Group 2. Which is the correct formula of calcium fluoride?
markScheme: 1 mark: CaF₂
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ needs two F⁻ ions to balance its charge: (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0, so CaF₂.

questions.question: Lithium (Group 1) reacts with oxygen (Group 6). How many lithium atoms react with each oxygen atom?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2
questions.explanation: Each Li atom loses 1 electron; an O atom needs 2. So 2 Li atoms give 1 electron each, forming Li₂O.

options: Dots are protons and crosses are electrons.
To show which atom each electron came from.
Crosses show electrons that are shared.
markScheme: 1 mark: To show which atom each electron came from.
questions.explanation: Dots and crosses are both electrons; using two symbols shows where each electron originated, so the transfer is clear.

questions.question: Which statement about the formation of magnesium oxide is correct?
options: Magnesium loses two electrons, which are transferred to oxygen.
Magnesium and oxygen share two pairs of electrons.
Oxygen loses two electrons to magnesium.
Magnesium gains two protons from oxygen.
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnesium loses two electrons, which are transferred to oxygen.
questions.explanation: Magnesium (Group 2) loses its two outer electrons to oxygen (Group 6), forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.

questions.question: Element Q forms an ion Q²⁻ with the electronic structure 2,8,8. Which element is Q?
markScheme: 1 mark: Sulfur
questions.explanation: Q²⁻ has 18 electrons and gained 2, so the atom had 16 electrons: sulfur (2,8,6). Calcium forms Ca²⁺ with 2,8,8, not a negative ion.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the electronic structures of two elements, X and Y.
X and Y react to form an ionic compound.
What is the formula of the compound formed between X and Y?
markScheme: 1 mark: XY₂
questions.explanation: X (Group 2) forms X²⁺ and Y (Group 7, fluorine) forms Y⁻. Two Y⁻ balance one X²⁺: XY₂ (this is MgF₂).

questions.question:
Potassium is in Group 1 of the periodic table.
How many electrons does a potassium atom lose when it forms a potassium ion?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1
questions.explanation: Group 1 atoms have one outer electron, which is lost to form K⁺.

questions.question:
The atomic number of potassium is 19.
How many electrons are in a potassium ion, K⁺?
markScheme: 1 mark: 18
questions.explanation: The atom has 19 electrons. A 1+ charge means one has been lost: 19 − 1 = 18. The ion has the argon structure 2,8,8.

questions.question:
The atomic number of chlorine is 17.
How many protons are in a chloride ion, Cl⁻?
markScheme: 1 mark: 17
questions.explanation: Forming an ion changes only the number of electrons. Cl⁻ still has 17 protons but now has 18 electrons.

questions.question:
Sodium is in Group 1 and oxygen is in Group 6.
Sodium reacts with oxygen to form sodium oxide, Na₂O.
Calculate the total number of electrons transferred from sodium atoms to one oxygen atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: two sodium atoms each give one electron / oxygen gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻
1 mark: 2
questions.explanation: Oxygen (Group 6) needs 2 electrons. Each sodium atom (Group 1) can give only 1, so two sodium atoms each transfer 1 electron: 2 electrons in total, forming Na₂O.

questions.question: State what happens to the electrons when a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: (outer shell) electrons are transferred / metal loses electrons
1 mark: from the metal atom to the non-metal atom / non-metal gains electrons
questions.explanation: This is the core of ionic bonding: electrons in the metal's outer shell move to the non-metal.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the groups of two elements.
Give the charge on the ion formed by each element.
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) 2+ / Ca²⁺
1 mark: (b) 2− / O²⁻
questions.explanation: Calcium loses its 2 outer electrons (2+). Oxygen gains 2 electrons to fill its outer shell (2−).

questions.question: Explain why a chloride ion has a negative charge.
markScheme: 1 mark: it has gained an electron so it has more electrons than protons
questions.explanation: Chlorine (17 protons) gains one electron to have 18 electrons; the extra negative charge makes the ion 1−.

questions.question: Give the electronic structures of a magnesium atom and a magnesium ion.
markScheme: 1 mark: Mg atom 2,8,2
1 mark: Mg²⁺ ion 2,8
questions.explanation: Magnesium has 12 electrons (2,8,2). Losing the 2 outer electrons gives 2,8, the same as neon.

markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium ion should be 2+ (Mg²⁺) because it is in Group 2 / loses 2 electrons
1 mark: there should be two chloride ions / two chlorine atoms each gain one electron
1 mark: MgCl₂
questions.explanation: Magnesium loses two electrons but each chlorine only needs one, so two chlorine atoms react with one magnesium atom.

questions.question: Suggest why Group 1 metals form 1+ ions rather than gaining 7 electrons to fill their outer shell.
markScheme: 1 mark: losing one electron leaves a full (outer) shell below
1 mark: it is much easier to lose 1 electron than to gain 7
questions.explanation: The outer electron is lost to leave the full shell underneath, giving a noble gas structure with far less energy needed than gaining seven electrons.

questions.question: Calcium sulfide has the formula CaS. Explain why the ratio of calcium ions to sulfide ions is 1 : 1.
markScheme: 1 mark: calcium forms Ca²⁺ (loses 2 electrons) and sulfur forms S²⁻ (gains 2 electrons)
1 mark: charges are equal and opposite / electrons lost equal electrons gained, so one of each
questions.explanation: Ca (Group 2) and S (Group 6) both move 2 electrons, so one calcium atom gives exactly what one sulfur atom needs.

questions.question: Describe, in terms of electrons, what happens when magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Give the electronic structures of the ions formed.
markScheme: Indicative content: magnesium is a metal (Group 2), oxygen a non-metal (Group 6); magnesium atom (2,8,2) loses two outer shell electrons; transferred to an oxygen atom (2,6); oxygen gains two electrons; Mg²⁺ ion (2,8) and O²⁻ ion (2,8); both have a full outer shell / neon electronic structure; oppositely charged ions attract strongly (ionic bond).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): transfer of two electrons from magnesium to oxygen clearly described, with correct ions, charges and electronic structures
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct statements, for example electrons lost by magnesium, or one correct ion, but incomplete or unclear direction
questions.explanation: Full answers state the number of electrons, the direction of transfer, the ion charges and the 2,8 structures, then link to attraction between opposite charges.

questions.question:
Potassium reacts with sulfur to form potassium sulfide.
Table 1 gives information about potassium and sulfur.
Explain how potassium sulfide forms.
Your answer should include:
• the electronic structures of the atoms and ions
• a description of the dot and cross diagram
• the formula of the compound.
markScheme: Indicative content: K is 2,8,8,1 and S is 2,8,6; each potassium atom loses its one outer electron; sulfur needs two electrons to fill its outer shell; so two potassium atoms each transfer one electron to one sulfur atom; ions K⁺ (2,8,8) and S²⁻ (2,8,8); both have argon electronic structure; dot and cross: two K atoms each with one ×, S with six •; arrows showing transfer; products [K]⁺ twice and [S]²⁻ with six • and two ×, in square brackets with charges; formula K₂S; oppositely charged ions attract by strong electrostatic forces.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered explanation including correct electronic structures, the 2 : 1 ratio, a correct description of the dot and cross diagram and the formula K₂S
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct description of electron transfer and ion charges with some electronic structures; the ratio or the diagram description may be incomplete
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic statements, for example potassium loses an electron or sulfur gains electrons, with little detail
questions.explanation: The key step is recognising that one sulfur atom needs two electrons but each potassium atom only provides one, so the formula is K₂S. Both ions end with 18 electrons (2,8,8).

questions.question: Compare the way sodium and chlorine atoms change when they form sodium chloride. Refer to protons, electrons and charges.
markScheme: Indicative content: sodium atom 11 protons, 11 electrons; loses 1 electron; Na⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons; positive charge; chlorine atom 17 protons, 17 electrons; gains 1 electron; Cl⁻ has 17 protons and 18 electrons; negative charge; number of protons unchanged in both; both end with full outer shells (2,8 and 2,8,8).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison of both atoms, including unchanged protons, the change in electrons and the resulting charges
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements that sodium loses and chlorine gains an electron, with limited detail
questions.explanation: A strong comparison links each change in electrons to the resulting charge, and notes that the proton numbers stay the same.
